title: How Japanese Whisky Is Made | Craft Beer School
desc: How Japanese whisky is made, from its Scottish roots to many still shapes, mizunara oak and the labelling standard Japan introduced in 2021.
teaser: Japanese whisky learned from Scotland, then built its own habits. Here is how it is actually made.
standfirst: Japanese whisky began as a careful study of Scotch and grew into a style of its own. Its distilleries make many different spirits under one roof, use a rare native oak and blend with great care. This guide explains the process and the rules behind the label.
sections:
Japanese whisky traces its start to the 1920s. Masataka Taketsuru studied whisky making in Scotland and brought that knowledge home, where he helped set up Japan's first commercial whisky production. The model was Scotch: malted barley, copper pot stills, oak casks and blending.

So the basic process is familiar. Malted barley is milled, mashed with hot water to make a sugary wort, fermented with yeast and distilled twice in pot stills. Grain whisky for blends comes from column stills. Our guide to how whisky is made covers those steps in detail.

Here Japan took its own path. In Scotland, blenders have long traded whisky between distilleries to get the variety they need. Japanese companies historically did very little of that trading. To build complex blends, they made the variety themselves.

A single Japanese distillery may run several still shapes and sizes, different yeast strains, different fermentation times and both peated and unpeated malt. Some use direct fired stills, some steam heated. The result is a library of distinct spirits under one roof, which the blender then combines. It is a very different way of working from the one distillery, one style habit of many Scotch malt distilleries.

Most Japanese whisky matures in the same cask types as Scotch: ex-bourbon barrels, sherry butts and refill casks. What sets Japan apart is mizunara, a Japanese oak. It is hard to work, porous and prone to leaking, so it is expensive and used sparingly, often for part of a blend or a finish.

Whisky aged in mizunara is often described as having sandalwood, incense and coconut notes. Those notes take time to develop, so mizunara is mostly found in older or premium releases.

For a long time Japan had loose rules on what could be called Japanese whisky. Some bottles contained imported whisky blended in Japan. In 2021 the Japan Spirits and Liqueurs Makers Association introduced a voluntary standard for its members. To be labelled Japanese whisky under it, the whisky must be:

  • made from malted grain, which may be combined with other cereals, using water drawn in Japan
  • fermented, distilled and matured in Japan
  • matured for at least three years in wooden casks
  • bottled in Japan at a minimum of 40% ABV

Producers had a transition period to comply. Check the label for the producer's own statement if you want to know where the whisky came from.

There is no single Japanese whisky flavour, because the distilleries make such a range. Many blends are light, clean and precise, with fruit, honey and gentle oak. Some single malts are rich with sherry. Others are smoky and coastal. The common thread most tasters note is balance: nothing shouts.

That lightness also explains the highball's popularity in Japan. Whisky with chilled soda over plenty of ice suits a light, aromatic blend. It is also a sensible way to drink whisky slowly in a hot climate, which makes it popular in Indian summers too.

Japanese distilleries sit in very different places, from cool mountain valleys to warmer areas near cities. Mountain sites have cool, soft water and slower maturation. Warmer warehouses mean faster interaction between spirit and wood and a higher loss to evaporation each year.

Fermentation is another lever. Some distilleries use wooden washbacks, which can harbour lactic bacteria that add depth and fruit over a longer fermentation. Others use stainless steel for cleaner, more controlled results. Each choice shows up in the new make.

Japanese whisky also went through a long boom in demand after years of weak sales, which left aged stock in short supply. That is why many releases carry no age statement. As with any whisky, the absence of a number says little about the liquid in the glass.

Pour 20 ml of a Japanese blend and 20 ml of a Scotch blend side by side. Nose both. The Japanese one will often be cleaner and more fruit led. Taste each neat, then with a few drops of water. Drink water between sips and keep the measures small.

Your first step: next time you see a Japanese whisky, read the back label for the words made in Japan or a statement about where it was distilled. Then taste it as the blender meant: slowly, with your attention on balance rather than power.
faqs: Masataka Taketsuru studied whisky making in Scotland and helped launch commercial whisky production in Japan in the 1920s.
A Japanese oak used for some whisky casks. It is hard to work and leaks easily, so it is used sparingly. It is linked to sandalwood and incense notes.
Is all Japanese whisky made in Japan?
Not always in the past. Since 2021 a voluntary industry standard requires whisky labelled Japanese whisky by member producers to be fermented, distilled, matured and bottled in Japan.
